query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of approximately 2 at% aluminum to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enable the in situ formation of a protective alumina scale at high temperatures, thereby enhancing oxygen resistance without degrading its useful mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding ~2 at% aluminum while keeping the balance as equiatomic Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
generation.conditions: Testing at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air or controlled O2 partial pressure) for prolonged exposures (e.g., 100 hours) with mechanical loading maintained within the strain rate range of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ or evaluated at room temperature post-exposure to verify ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The added aluminum preferentially oxidizes on the surface to form a dense and stable alumina scale that acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress. This protective layer impedes the rapid oxidation of the underlying alloy, thereby maintaining its high-temperature mechanical properties while significantly improving oxygen resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance due to the protective alumina scale formation, with mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) remaining comparable to the untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which displays high-temperature yield strengths of 163–530 MPa and 8–16% tensile ductility but suffers from poor oxygen resistance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be beneficial under high-temperature conditions (around 1000 °C) and oxidizing environments; its effect on other temperature ranges or under different mechanical loading rates may vary.
generation.uncertainty: The precise amount of aluminum needed, the uniformity and long-term stability of the alumina layer under cyclic thermal/mechanical loading, and any minor trade-offs in ductility due to microstructural changes remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a second set modified with ~2 at% aluminum. Expose both sets to an oxidizing atmosphere at 1000 °C for 100 hours followed by comprehensive mechanical testing (tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C) and surface analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS, XRD) to assess oxide layer formation and mechanical integrity.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS, XRD)
Yield strength and tensile ductility at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified alloy does not show a significantly improved resistance to oxidation (evidenced by similar or higher oxide scale thickness/weight gain) and/or if the beneficial mechanical properties (i.e., yield strength and ductility) are degraded compared to the baseline alloy after exposure, the hypothesis will be falsified.
